answers.text: Three lines, always the same order — delivery date, item and quantity, and any change from the original order. That fixed order is what keeps it consistent, I think.
List each claim by date, amount, category and submitter, then total the amounts at the end — that way the total should match no matter who runs it.
The dates don't quite work — 'three days out from today' doesn't match the 19th being the revised date. I'd want to check the original call date.
62 up from 54 is about right for a 15% rise. But 3 late out of 62 isn't 97%, more like 95% — I'd flag that before it's sent up.
I'd sign off on Output 2, it shows the €612,000 and €25,100 behind the 4.1%. Output 1 doesn't show any of that.
Reply 2 — it has the order and credit references, so it's traceable. Reply 1 might well be true, I just wouldn't send it without something to check first.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. No, still cautious with an unvetted tool. 5. No.
I'd redact the pricing terms, and I'd be careful with the confidentiality clause too since it names both companies.
Before the report goes to the manager, I'd cross-check the totals against the warehouse system.
Step 1 matters because a bad read carries through, and step 4 — the automatic send — is where I'd want a gate too, since that's the point you can't take back.
